label: Theorem-readiness of a mathematical-biology claim, v0.1.0
description: Scores how close a claim from mathematical biology is to a theorem that is also an empirically testable statement about living systems. A claim reaches 'theorem status' in the strong sense when (a) it is a precise mathematical proposition, (b) it is proved from stated assumptions, and (c) those assumptions are empirically checkable and hold, or fail, in identifiable biological systems. Each dimension is scored in [0,1] as a graded judgement (delphi:hasScore), never as a probability. The overall score is the weighted mean of the five dimensions.

dimensions.question: Can the claim be written as an unambiguous mathematical proposition (definitions, quantifiers, hypotheses) without loss of what the author meant?

anchors.0.0: metaphor or slogan with no agreed formal reading
anchors.0.5: several competing formalizations, or a formal core plus informal surplus
anchors.1.0: a single canonical formal statement exists and is accepted

dimensions.question: Within its formal reading, is the claim proved, plausibly provable, open, or false? Machine-checked proofs (Lean, Coq, Isabelle, mathlib) count higher than paper proofs only if the checked statement is the claim itself, not a generic arithmetic lemma.

anchors.0.0: no mathematical content to prove, or shown false as stated
anchors.0.3: open conjecture with weak partial results
anchors.0.6: proved for special cases or under strong idealizations
anchors.0.85: proved in full generality on paper and widely accepted

dimensions.question: Does the claim make falsifiable predictions about measurable biological quantities, with a feasible experiment or dataset that could refute it?

anchors.0.5: testable only qualitatively, or only with infeasible experiments
anchors.1.0: sharp quantitative predictions with standard, feasible tests

dimensions.question: Has the claim survived serious empirical tests in real biological systems?

anchors.1.0: repeatedly confirmed across systems and labs

dimensions.question: If the mathematical statement is a theorem, do its hypotheses actually hold in the biological systems it is meant to describe, so that the theorem says something true about biology rather than only about the model?

anchors.0.0: assumptions are known not to hold anywhere relevant
anchors.0.5: assumptions hold approximately in some systems
anchors.1.0: assumptions are routinely verified to hold

verdicts.theorem-and-validated: proved, testable and empirically supported with faithful assumptions
verdicts.theorem-ready: precise and testable; a proof exists or is within reach; bridge needs work
verdicts.model-theorem-only: proved inside its model, but weak testability or bridge fidelity
verdicts.testable-not-formal: empirically sharp but not a mathematical proposition
verdicts.conjectural-framework: neither precise nor sharply testable yet
